final_answer: No, the trial court did not err (assuming Texas law and a mandamus-type review of the disqualification order). The facts track In re Zaidi, No. 24-0245 (Tex. 2026) (Devine, J.; mandamus denied), which applies Texas's bright-line rule for side-switching nonlawyer staff. (1) Under Phoenix Founders v. Marshall, In re American Home Products and In re Columbia Valley Healthcare (Tex. 2010), when a legal assistant worked on a matter for one side and then works on the same matter for the opposing firm, there is a conclusive presumption that she obtained confidences (here: hundreds of privileged communications, strategy meetings) and a rebuttable presumption that she shared them with the new firm. The shared-confidences presumption is rebutted only by prophylactic measures, not by denials of disclosure or lack of memory: the firm must (a) instruct/admonish the assistant not to work on the matter and (b) take other reasonable steps to shield her from it. If she actually works on the matter, disqualification of the firm follows. (2) Smith Fullingham did no screening or admonishment when it hired her in 2017 and did not ask about her past; she then worked on the Apex-Prestige matter on 13 occasions and e-filed two documents in 2022. Per Zaidi, even where the employee was not switching sides at hiring (a later-arising conflict), the firm must admonish her at or before the time she begins work on the conflicted matter; the firm's post-inquiry 2023 screening, its assertion that she did not recall, and its assertion that no confidences were shared come too late and are legally insufficient. The limited, secretarial and sporadic nature of her work does not matter under the bright-line rule. (3) Waiver: the delay defense fails. Waiver requires unreasonable delay after the movant knew of the conflict; Zaidi held that e-filing notifications bearing her name did not conclusively establish actual knowledge of her prior involvement or unreasonable delay (at most evidence for the trial court to weigh). Apex moved within about two months of learning (Jan to early March 2023), which is prompt; the trial court's implied finding of no waiver is within its discretion. (4) Caveats: I could not open the full opinion text (egress blocked) and relied on search-result summaries of Zaidi and Columbia Valley; Zaidi's specifics were drawn from secondary summaries, and Phoenix Founders/American Home Products were not independently retrieved. Disqualification is also reviewed for abuse of discretion; mandamus is available because there is no adequate appeal remedy. Under this authority, the trial court's order should stand.

claims.text: The trial court did not err in disqualifying Smith Fullingham.
Conclusive presumption of confidences and rebuttable presumption of sharing apply; rebutted only by admonishment and shielding, not denial or lack of recollection.
Lack of admonishment before she began work on the matter, and only belated screening, does not avoid disqualification.
E-filing notices bearing her name do not conclusively establish waiver; movant's prompt motion about two months after learning defeats delay argument.
